channel.title: Shrine on Japan Specialty Traveler
channel.description: Recent content in Shrine on Japan Specialty Traveler

item.title: Aoshima Island — Guide
item.description: Aoshima is a small, subtropical island just off the coast of Miyazaki city, connected to the mainland by a footbridge and famous for its natural beauty and romantic shrine. The little island is entirely covered in a lush jungle of some 5,000 betel palms and subtropical plants, giving it an exotic, southern-island feel. Ringing the island is one of its most striking features: the ‘Oni no Sentakuita’ or ‘Devil’s Washboard’, vast wave-cut platforms of ridged rock that radiate out into the sea in remarkable regular corrugations, exposed at low tide.

item.title: Arita: Birthplace of Japanese Porcelain — Guide
item.description: Arita is the birthplace of Japanese porcelain, where the first true porcelain in Japan was fired in the early 1600s after kaolin clay was discovered nearby. For over four centuries the town has produced Arita-yaki (also known as Imari ware), refined white porcelain painted in cobalt blue and vivid overglaze colours, exported around the world and prized to this day. The town is a living museum of ceramics: porcelain museums display masterpieces old and new, historic kilns and shops line the streets, and Tozan Shrine, the potters' guardian, is famous for its unique torii gate, lanterns and railings all made of blue-and-white porcelain.

item.title: Dazaifu Tenmangu: Shrine of Learning — Guide
item.description: Dazaifu Tenmangu, just outside Fukuoka city, is one of the most revered shrines in Japan, dedicated to Sugawara no Michizane, the Heian-era scholar-official deified as Tenjin, the god of learning. Students from across the country come to pray for success in exams, and the beautiful grounds are famous for their plum trees — Michizane’s favourite — which bloom in late winter, including a legendary ‘flying plum’ said to have flown from Kyoto to be near him.

item.title: Himure & Akahage Shrines, Bungo-ono — Guide
item.description: In the rural inland region of Bungo-ono in Oita, small local shrines set amid forest, rock and countryside offer a peaceful, authentic experience of rural Shinto worship away from the crowds. Bungo-ono is a landscape shaped by ancient volcanic activity from nearby Mount Aso, giving it dramatic gorges, waterfalls, rock formations and rich soil — a designated UNESCO Global Geopark. Its shrines, often tucked into atmospheric natural settings among old trees, mossy stone and streams, reflect the deep-rooted local connection between the community, the land and its deities.

item.title: Inland Mountain Shrines & Temples — Guide
item.description: Beyond the famous coast and Takachiho, the forested mountains of inland Miyazaki hold atmospheric shrines and temple complexes that offer a quiet, spiritual escape into nature. Set amid ancient cedars, mossy stone steps, streams and mountain scenery, these sacred sites carry a deep sense of age and tranquillity, reflecting the long-rooted local traditions of mountain worship that thread through this region. Weathered wooden halls, torii gates, guardian statues and secluded settings reward visitors who venture inland with a peaceful, contemplative atmosphere that changes beautifully with the seasons — fresh green in spring and summer, brilliant colour in autumn.

item.title: Kanda Matsuri — Guide
item.description: The Kanda Matsuri, centred on Kanda Myojin Shrine, is one of Tokyo’s three great Shinto festivals (alongside the Sanja and Sanno matsuri) and dates back to the Edo period, when it was celebrated as a display of prosperity under the Tokugawa shogunate. The festival’s grandest events are held in full scale only in odd-numbered years (alternating with the Sanno Matsuri), over several days in mid-May. Its highlight is a spectacular day-long procession that winds for kilometres through the Kanda, Nihonbashi and Otemachi districts of central Tokyo — a long parade featuring people in Heian-era court costume, priests on horseback, musicians, dancers and floats, followed on another day by around a hundred mikoshi (portable shrines) carried energetically through the streets to the shrine.

item.title: Kotohiragu Shrine: The 785-Step Climb — Guide
item.description: Kotohiragu, affectionately known as Konpira-san, is one of Japan’s most beloved shrines, dedicated to the guardian deity of seafarers and long a pilgrimage destination drawing visitors from across the country. It sits high on the wooded slopes of Mount Zozu above the town of Kotohira, and reaching it is famously a climb: a stone stairway of 785 steps to the main shrine, or 1,368 all the way to the inner shrine.

item.title: Kyoto Setsubun: Driving Out Demons in Early February — Guide
item.description: Setsubun, held around 3 February, marks the eve of spring in the old lunar calendar and is celebrated across Japan with mame-maki, the throwing of roasted soybeans to drive out bad fortune, shouting ‘oni wa soto, fuku wa uchi’ — demons out, luck in. Kyoto keeps the day with particular richness: its major shrines and temples host their own ceremonies, from costumed oni demons chased away with beans at Yoshida and Rozanji, to bean-throwing led by geiko and maiko at Yasaka Shrine, to fire rituals and huge crowds scrambling for thrown packets of beans and prizes.

item.title: Miyajidake Shrine and the Path of Light — Guide
item.description: Miyajidake Shrine in Fukutsu, between Fukuoka and Kitakyushu, is a much-loved shrine famous for several superlatives. It holds an enormous shimenawa (sacred straw rope) — one of the largest in Japan, several metres thick and weighing tonnes — along with a giant drum and bell. Its greatest fame, however, comes twice a year, in late February and late October, when the setting sun aligns perfectly with the shrine’s long, straight stone approach that runs down toward the sea, creating the spectacular ‘Path of Light’ (Hikari no Michi) — a golden road of sunlight stretching to the horizon, drawing huge crowds.

item.title: Mount Mitake — Guide
item.description: Mount Mitake (Mitake-san), rising about 929 m in the Okutama region of western Tokyo, is a long-revered sacred mountain and a wonderful nature and hiking escape within the metropolis. A cable car whisks visitors up much of the mountain, near the top of which sits a small, atmospheric village of pilgrim lodgings (shukubo) and shops, and the venerable Musashi-Mitake Shrine, reached by a final flight of stone steps and offering fine views.

item.title: Osaka Tenmangu: Shrine of Scholars and the Tenjin Festival — Guide
item.description: Osaka Tenmangu enshrines Sugawara no Michizane, the ninth-century scholar-official deified as Tenjin, the god of learning, and it has drawn students praying for examination success for over a thousand years. Founded in 949, the shrine sits at the head of one of the longest shopping arcades in Japan and is the spiritual home of the Tenjin Matsuri, held each July — one of the three great festivals of Japan, in which sacred palanquins are carried to the river and paraded on a flotilla of boats beneath fireworks.

item.title: Sekiya Shrine and Its Hidden Waterfall — Guide
item.description: Tucked into the forested hills of western Tottori, Sekiya Shrine and its hidden waterfall are the kind of quiet, off-the-map spot that rewards travellers willing to leave the main sights behind. A modest shrine sits among old trees, its approach cool and green, and a waterfall tumbles nearby, the sound of falling water and birdsong the only company. There are no crowds and no ticket gates — just a peaceful, faintly sacred atmosphere of the sort that once drew mountain ascetics to places like this across the San’in region.

item.title: Tatsuda Shrine — Guide
item.description: Tatsuda Shrine is a serene Shinto shrine in Kumamoto, tucked among woodland and greenery in a quiet setting away from the city bustle. Approached through torii gates and shaded paths, its wooden shrine buildings, mossy stone lanterns and forested grounds create a calm, spiritual atmosphere, especially beautiful in the fresh green of early summer and the coloured leaves of autumn. The Tatsuda area is historically associated with the ruling Hosokawa clan, whose family temple and gardens lie nearby, adding a layer of samurai-era heritage to a visit.

item.title: Hydrangea Season in Wakayama: Blue Blooms in the Rains — Guide
item.description: June, the rainy season, is hydrangea (ajisai) season in Japan, and Wakayama’s shrines, temples and hillside gardens fill with thousands of blooms in shifting blues, purples, pinks and whites. Hydrangeas are the flower of the rains — they look their best when wet, the colours deepening and the heavy heads bowing under raindrops — so this is one of the few times when a grey, drizzly day genuinely improves the view.

item.title: Kunozan Toshogu: The Original Resting Place of Tokugawa Ieyasu — Guide
item.description: Kunozan Toshogu is the original shrine of Tokugawa Ieyasu, founder of the Tokugawa shogunate, built on Mount Kuno overlooking Suruga Bay immediately after his death in 1616 as his first burial place, before his remains were later enshrined at the more famous Nikko. Its brilliantly ornate halls, decorated with lacquer, gold leaf and intricate carvings, are designated National Treasures and predate Nikko’s, and the shrine is reached either by a scenic ropeway from the Nihondaira plateau or by climbing more than 1,100 stone steps up from the coast below.

item.title: Iwakiyama Shrine: the 'Nikko of the North' — Aomori Guide
item.description: At the foot of sacred Mt. Iwaki, the 1,200-year-old Iwakiyama Shrine is the spiritual heart of the Tsugaru region. Its ornately carved gates and halls, rich with colour and detail, have earned it the nickname the ‘Nikko of Oku’ — the Nikko of the far north. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hirosaki, Aomori Hours Grounds always open Admission Free Time needed About 1 hour Best time Autumn; also summer climbing season What to See The lavishly carved main gate (romon) and halls.

item.title: Morioka Hachimangu Shrine: The City Guardian — Guide
item.description: Morioka Hachimangu is the grand vermilion guardian shrine of the city — a lively centre of Morioka’s festival calendar, including the arrival of the decorated horses of Chagu-Chagu Umakko in June and a colourful autumn festival. Its bright halls and busy shrine grounds make it a warm, living counterpoint to the city’s museums. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Morioka, Iwate Hours Grounds always open Admission Free Time needed About 40 min Best time Festival days; year-round What to See The grand vermilion main hall.

item.title: Fushimi Inari Taisha Guide: Climbing the Thousand Torii Gates
item.description: There is no image of Kyoto more famous than the endless corridor of vermilion torii gates winding up a forested hillside at Fushimi Inari Taisha. Thousands of them — donated over centuries by businesses and individuals — form glowing tunnels that climb the sacred Mount Inari. It is one of the most photographed places in Japan, free to enter, open 24 hours, and far larger and more rewarding than most visitors realise: nearly everyone turns back after the first photogenic stretch, missing the quiet, atmospheric mountain shrine above.

item.title: Sumiyoshi Taisha Guide: Osaka's Ancient Shrine & Drum Bridge
item.description: The head shrine of some 2,300 Sumiyoshi shrines across Japan, Sumiyoshi Taisha is one of the country’s oldest and most distinctive Shinto sites — founded in the 3rd century, long before Buddhist influence reached Japan, and built in a rare ancient style found nowhere else. Its image is the steep, vermilion Taiko-bashi (drum bridge) arching over a pond, one of Osaka’s most photographed scenes. Revered as a guardian of sea travel and a bringer of good fortune, it draws over two million worshippers at New Year alone.

item.title: Shimane Girls' Trip: Onsen Retreats, Love Shrines & Garden Escapes
item.description: Shimane has been drawing Japanese women in groups for centuries — not as a modern travel trend, but because it holds two of the country’s most significant shrines for love, relationships, and human connection. Add restorative onsen with a legendary reputation for skin beauty, traditional sweet-making workshops, and a peony garden that peaks in spring, and you have a prefecture that delivers without trying hard. Izumo Taisha: Japan’s Matchmaking Grand Shrine Izumo Taisha is not a romantic tourist novelty.

item.title: Shimane Power Spots: Izumo Taisha, Sacred Shrines & Japan's Spiritual Heart
item.description: Japan has hundreds of sacred sites, but Shimane holds a different status entirely. This is the land described in the Kojiki — Japan’s oldest chronicle, written in 712 — as the place where the gods created the Japanese archipelago, where Susanoo slew the eight-headed serpent, and where Okuninushi built civilization before ceding it to the heavenly deities. Every October, the rest of Japan empties of its gods (the month is called Kannazuki, “month without gods”), because they have all traveled to Izumo for an assembly.

item.title: Shimane Solo Travel Guide: Ancient Shrines, Overnight Trains & Sea of Japan Solitude
item.description: Shimane draws almost no foreign crowds. That’s not a warning — it’s the point. If you’re traveling solo, this is exactly the kind of prefecture where you can sit in a tea room at a 1,600-year-old shrine without nudging anyone for space. The pace is unhurried. Locals are curious and warm. The landscape swings from castle moats to sea cliffs to UNESCO mining towns. For solo travelers who want authentic Japan without performance, Shimane delivers.

item.title: Top Sightseeing in Shimane: Izumo Taisha, Matsue Castle & Adachi Museum
item.description: Shimane Prefecture sits on Japan’s San’in coast, tucked away from the main tourist trails. That obscurity is precisely the point. No crowds at Izumo Taisha on a winter morning. Space to stand in silence before Matsue Castle’s black wooden keep. A seat at a window in the Adachi Museum while ranked gardens stretch out like a living scroll painting. Shimane rewards travelers who make the effort to get there. Izumo Taisha: Japan’s Oldest Grand Shrine Izumo Taisha is not merely old — it is the oldest documented shrine in Japan, predating the formal introduction of Buddhism.

item.title: Tottori Power Spots: Nageire-do Temple, Sacred Mountains & Ancient Shrines
item.description: Tottori prefecture does not shout about its spiritual heritage. It does not need to. The sites are so old, so physically demanding, and so embedded in the deep layers of Japanese myth that they speak for themselves. A cliff temple that appears to defy gravity. A beach where one of Japan’s oldest myths was enacted. A shrine to a minister who allegedly lived past three hundred years. And a sacred mountain that has absorbed more than twelve centuries of prayer.

item.title: Ise Jingu Complete Guide: Japan's Most Sacred Shrine
item.description: Ise Jingu stands apart from every other sacred site in Japan. Not by scale — there are shrine complexes that cover more ground — but by the nature of its significance. For over 2,000 years, Ise has been the spiritual centre of the Japanese nation, the home of Amaterasu Omikami, the sun goddess from whom the imperial family traces its divine lineage. The Emperor of Japan makes a personal visit to Ise at the beginning of each reign.

item.title: Kashima Jingu: Complete Guide to Ibaraki's Ancient Shrine
item.description: In a prefecture better known abroad for blue nemophila fields and a giant Buddha, Kashima Jingu stands apart as one of Japan’s most historically charged sacred sites. Buried deep in a forest of ancient Japanese cedar on the Pacific coast of eastern Ibaraki, the shrine predates written Japanese history. It was founded, according to tradition, in the reign of the legendary Emperor Jimmu, making it roughly contemporary with the origin myths of the Japanese state itself.
